summary: First English narrative for the National Security Council's 22 July 1948 decision to expand the Berlin airlift rather than send General Clay's proposed armed convoy, written from the case's verified facts (FRUS 1948 vol. II, docs 577, 581, 582, 586, 591; Office of the Historian).

narrative.hook: It is 22 July 1948, and the President is chairing the National Security Council. Half of Berlin has been cut off by land for four weeks. The general who runs occupied Germany wants to send an armed convoy down the road; the ambassador in Moscow warns that it could start a war.
narrative.short_setup: Since 24 June, Soviet forces have blocked every rail, road and canal route into the western sectors of Berlin, which sit deep inside the Soviet zone of Germany. The only links the Western Allies still have by written agreement are the air corridors, and since 26 June American transport planes have been flying supplies in, joined two days later by the British. No one knows whether air supply can keep the city going, especially once winter comes. The Red Army around Berlin vastly outnumbers the Western Allies' forces. On 10 July General Lucius Clay, the U.S. Military Governor, proposed telling the Soviets that on a fixed date a convoy with engineers and bridging equipment would reopen the road. The U.S. political adviser in Berlin, Murphy, agreed. A Soviet note on 14 July, which President Truman read as a total rejection, and a warning from the U.S. ambassador in Moscow followed. Clay and Murphy have now been summoned to Washington.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: Clay's argument was direct. The West had a right of access to Berlin, and the Soviets were justifying the blockade by citing 'technical difficulties'. If the Allies offered to fix those difficulties themselves and sent a convoy on a named date, the Soviets would have to either let it through or openly use force. Clay was convinced they did not want war, and that Berlin by itself was not worth a war to them unless they were already committed to one, in which case pressure would come somewhere else anyway. Clay also warned that months of waiting, especially into the winter, could let the city's situation deteriorate badly. In Berlin, Murphy reported, the idea of guarded convoys had almost universal support among British, French and German opinion.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: A convoy, as Clay admitted, carried an inherent risk: once it crossed into the Soviet zone it was committed. If it was stopped by force, the choice would be between a humiliating retreat and a shooting war, only three years after the last one, with Western forces around Berlin heavily outnumbered. The U.S. ambassador in Moscow judged after the Soviet note that the danger of armed conflict had grown and that an armed convoy would run a serious risk of precipitating war. The air corridors, by contrast, rested on written agreements. Supplying the city by air meant staying in Berlin without being the first to use force; if the Soviets tried to stop an unarmed supply flight, the onus of starting a conflict would be on them. It also bought time for diplomacy.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: The National Security Council, meeting with the President, decided to increase the airlift substantially by adding 75 C-54 transport aircraft. It reiterated the determination of the United States to remain in Berlin and agreed to build a new airfield in the city. The armed convoy was not ordered. A week later, on 28 July, the Joint Chiefs of Staff put their view in writing: they did not recommend supplying Berlin by armed convoy because of the risk of war and the inadequacy of American preparation for a global conflict, though they thought it prudent to plan for one as a last resort.
narrative.outcome_story: The airlift held, and then grew. It became steadily more efficient; at its height a plane landed at Tempelhof every 45 seconds. The city's politics did not stand still: in September 1948, after the Communist-led SED forced the Berlin city council to adjourn, around 300,000 West Berliners gathered at the Reichstag to protest against Soviet domination. By spring 1949 the Western Allies had shown they could sustain the operation indefinitely, while their own counter-blockade was causing severe shortages in the Soviet zone. In May 1949 the Soviets lifted the blockade. Shortly before, the Western Allies had created NATO; two weeks after, the West German state was established.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
Because the airlift worked, it is easy to treat the decision as obviously right and Clay's convoy as obviously reckless. Neither judgment follows from the outcome.

On decision quality, the choice rates as reasonable. Its core logic was sound: it kept the West in Berlin while leaving the first use of force to the other side, and it avoided a move that, once begun, could not be taken back. But it had a real weakness at the time it was made. Nobody knew whether aircraft could carry a city through a winter, and Clay, the person closest to the problem, had warned that a long wait could let the situation deteriorate. The decision accepted a slow, uncertain path with no guarantee it would be enough. It was also not a final rejection of force: the military chiefs advised planning for a convoy as a last resort.

On outcome quality, the result was good: the city was supplied, the blockade ended, and no war followed. But the success depended on things the Council could not control on 22 July. The airlift had to scale up as hoped, the Soviets had to refrain from attacking the air corridors, and Berliners had to hold firm, as they showed in September. The Western counter-blockade also added pressure on the other side.

As for Clay, the convoy's case was not foolish. Clay may even have been right that the Soviets would have let it through. But that bet could only be tested once, and losing it meant war. The decision did not prove Clay wrong. It chose not to find out.
narrative.decision_principle: When one option can be reversed and the other cannot, the reversible one deserves extra weight, even if it is slower and less certain to work, so long as it keeps the stronger option available for later.
narrative.longform_story:
In the summer of 1948 Berlin was a city divided four ways and surrounded by one. After the war, the victorious powers had split Germany into zones of occupation and Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, into sectors. As relations between the Western Allies and the Soviet Union soured, the city became the place where the quarrel would be tested.

In June the Americans and British introduced a new currency, the Deutschmark, into their zones and into West Berlin. The Soviets answered with a currency of their own, and on 24 June they closed every rail, road and canal route into the western sectors. The western half of a city still in ruins from the war faced the prospect of running out of food and fuel.

The only routes the Western Allies still held under written agreements were the air corridors from western Germany. On 26 June American transport planes began flying in supplies; the British followed two days later. It was a stopgap. No one knew whether aircraft could carry what a city needed, and the problem would get much harder when winter came. On the ground, the Red Army around Berlin dwarfed the Western Allies' forces.

General Lucius Clay, the American Military Governor, had already made the stakes clear. In June Clay had reported that remaining in Berlin was essential to American prestige in Germany and in Europe; it had become a symbol of American intent. On 10 July Clay went further. If the blockade went on, Clay argued, the Soviets should be told that on a specific date a convoy, with the bridging equipment needed to repair the supposedly broken route, would drive into Berlin. Clay admitted the risk: once the convoy crossed the border, it was committed. But Clay was convinced the Soviets did not want war and that the convoy would get through. The next day Murphy, the American political adviser in Berlin, backed guarded convoys with troops and engineers, reporting that the idea had almost universal support among British, French and German opinion in the city.

In Washington the picture looked darker. On 14 July a Soviet note arrived that President Truman considered a total rejection of everything the West had asked. From Moscow, Ambassador Smith reported that the danger of armed conflict had grown, and that sending an armed convoy to break the blockade would run a serious risk of precipitating war. Clay and Murphy were summoned home. On 22 July the National Security Council met, with the President presiding, to decide.

The choice was stark. A convoy would test Soviet resolve directly. If Clay was right, it might end the blockade in days and spare the city a winter of uncertainty. If Clay was wrong, American soldiers could be fighting Soviet soldiers on a road in eastern Germany, and the West would face either a humiliating retreat or a new war with too few troops. The airlift, by contrast, risked nothing irreversible. It used corridors guaranteed in writing, and any Soviet attempt to stop it would make the Soviets the aggressors against an unarmed humanitarian effort. But it might simply not be enough.

The Council chose the air. It agreed to add 75 C-54 transport planes to the airlift, reaffirmed that the United States would remain in Berlin, and agreed to build a new airfield in the city. A week later the Joint Chiefs of Staff explained their view: they did not recommend supply by armed convoy because of the risk of war and how unprepared the country was for a global conflict, though they thought it wise to plan for one as a last resort.

The airlift grew into something no one had quite imagined. It became steadily more efficient, until at its height a plane was landing at Tempelhof every 45 seconds. The pressure was not only military. In September, after the Communist-led SED forced Berlin's city council to adjourn, some 300,000 West Berliners gathered before the Reichstag to protest against Soviet domination, and their turnout helped convince the West to keep going. By spring 1949 the Allies had shown they could sustain the airlift indefinitely, while their counter-blockade was causing severe shortages in the Soviet zone. In May 1949 the Soviets lifted the blockade. NATO had been founded shortly before, and two weeks later the West German state came into being.

Looking back, the airlift is remembered as a triumph, and it is tempting to cast Clay's convoy as the reckless road not taken. That is too easy. On 22 July no one knew the airlift would work; Clay's warning about the winter was a reasonable fear. And Clay might have been right that the Soviets would not shoot. What made the Council's choice sound was not that it guaranteed success, but that it avoided a step that could not be undone, while keeping a harder option in reserve. The good outcome came from that choice, and also from things no one controlled on that day: the airlift's growth, Soviet restraint in the air, and the steadiness of the people of Berlin.
